The replacement model

One archive. Two futures.

Today, hybrid builds make the library useful before it is complete. Standalone is the longer climb to owning the entire runtime.

Hybrid · use it now

Link a static archive into your C program. Nelibc exports replace matching functions; uncovered names continue to resolve from the chosen host libc. Zig cc is the default toolchain, with GCC and optional TinyCC shootouts.

Standalone · build toward it

A separate Linux x86-64 profile grows its own startup, syscalls, allocation, threads, process, locale, and I/O paths. It has real working slices; it is not yet a general-purpose drop-in libc.

Try the hybrid build

Start in two commands.

Install Nelua and Zig first. The dogfood target builds Nelibc, links a C consumer, runs it, and checks that Nelibc symbols reached the executable.

git clone https://github.com/Spaceghost/nelibc.git
cd nelibc && make dogfood-zig

The quickstart also covers GCC, musl, and optional TinyCC profiles.

What dogfooding means

The C caller stays ordinary. Build with `-fno-builtin` when checking a symbol so the compiler does not replace the function call with an intrinsic.

The host libc stays useful. Hybrid archives add Nelibc implementations while uncovered APIs continue to resolve against glibc or musl.

The standalone path stays honest. It is a separate profile with gaps; the README and roadmap track those gaps directly.

What remains

Core work, ranked.

A compelling replacement depends on trusted behavior and broad consumers, not just an impressive exported-name count.
